primary_cause: Macro risk-off plus concern that pandemic volume mix would hurt margins not help them. No major UPS-specific headline in April 1-3
secondary_factors: Logistics disruption and uncertainty about 2020 outlook with commercial package demand falling even as home deliveries rose
store_description: UPS fell 3.3% even though home-delivery demand was rising because investors were focusing on margin quality not just volume. Later disclosures showed UPS withdrew 2020 guidance and said Q1 profit fell 13% which fits the market's early-April fear that COVID was distorting the business mix.

primary_cause: Mostly macro selloff not a fresh UNH-specific negative. No major UNH-specific headline in April 1-3
secondary_factors: Uncertainty around medical claims deferred care and recession-driven membership/employer-coverage risk
store_description: UNH dropped 4.6% even though the company did not release a new negative headline. The market was likely discounting recession risk and uncertainty around how COVID treatment costs delayed procedures and employer-sponsored insurance losses would net out.

primary_cause: Collapse in ride-hailing demand from COVID lockdowns. Core rides business was already under pressure with rides down roughly 60% to 70% in some markets
secondary_factors: Investor concern about layoffs/cost cuts and uncertainty about the path to profitability
store_description: Uber's 3.6% decline looks mainly tied to the market continuing to reprice a business whose core mobility volumes had cratered by roughly 60% to 70% in some cities. Delivery demand was improving but was not yet enough to offset the shock to the much larger rides segment.

primary_cause: Macro selloff with added concern about WarnerMedia's COVID exposure. No material AT&T-specific headline in April 1-3
secondary_factors: High debt pay-TV pressure weaker advertising and movie release delays
store_description: AT&T's 4.5% drop does not appear tied to a fresh headline but investors had reason to worry that the pandemic would pressure both media revenue and already-weak legacy businesses. Later results showed COVID shaved about $2.0 billion to $2.8 billion from WarnerMedia-related revenue.

primary_cause: Broad market selloff. No material Southern-specific headline in April 1-3
secondary_factors: Utility-specific worries about lower commercial/industrial demand and general recession stress
store_description: Southern's 4.1% decline looks mostly like a risk-off move rather than a response to company news. The payroll shock pushed investors to reprice even defensive names amid concern that business shutdowns would pressure power demand and collections.

primary_cause: Fresh confirmation that store restrictions and labor-cost support would continue longer. Starbucks announced on April 1 it would extend special COVID provisions for U.S. workers and keep dining areas closed through May 3
secondary_factors: Broader payroll-driven risk-off and fears about traffic reduced hours and margin compression
store_description: Starbucks fell 3.0% after telling investors on April 1 that pandemic operating restrictions and worker support measures would continue for at least two more weeks. Later Q2 results showed revenue down 5% to $6.0 billion confirming investors were correctly bracing for a sharp COVID hit.

primary_cause: Macro selloff plus smartphone-demand worries. No major Qualcomm-specific headline in April 1-3
secondary_factors: Broader semiconductor demand uncertainty and ongoing regulatory overhang
store_description: Qualcomm's 4.1% decline looks mostly like a macro move but it hit a stock already exposed to fears of weaker handset demand during global lockdowns. Reuters later noted near-term uncertainty in smartphone demand and supply due to COVID.

primary_cause: Broad software selloff within the payroll-shock market decline. No material company-specific negative in April 1-3
secondary_factors: Concern that enterprises would freeze projects or delay IT spending despite increased need for digital workflow tools
store_description: ServiceNow's 3.6% drop appears to have been mostly valuation compression and general risk-off rather than a fresh company event. Investors were still debating whether mission-critical enterprise software would prove resilient or face delayed deal cycles.

primary_cause: Macro selloff plus semiconductor-demand uncertainty. No major AMD-specific headline in April 1-3
secondary_factors: PC/server strength helped but investors worried about broader electronics and cyclical demand weakness
store_description: AMD's 4.3% decline looks more like a risk-off semiconductor move than a reaction to a new company headline. The market was balancing areas of resilience such as data center and work-from-home PC demand against global recession risk.

primary_cause: Broad market selloff with concern about delayed tax-filing season disrupting TurboTax revenue cadence. IRS had pushed tax filing deadline from April 15 to July 15
secondary_factors: Concern about timing disruption to seasonal tax-software revenue
store_description: Intuit fell 3.0% mainly in a weak tape but the deadline change also muddied the usual seasonal earnings pattern for TurboTax-related revenue. The issue was less that demand vanished and more that investors temporarily lost clarity on timing and execution.

primary_cause: Broad market selloff. No major IBM-specific headline in April 1-3
secondary_factors: Fear that enterprise IT spending and consulting demand would weaken in a deep recession
store_description: IBM's 3.3% drop appears to have been mostly macro and sector-driven with investors de-risking mature IT names exposed to slower corporate spending. No clean IBM-specific catalyst in the three-day window.

primary_cause: Market repricing of aerospace exposure. No fresh Honeywell headline in April 1-3 but the company was highly exposed to aerospace demand destruction
secondary_factors: General industrial recession fears and payroll-shock selling
store_description: Honeywell's 4.0% drop looks tied to investors increasingly appreciating how badly aerospace would be hit by COVID. Later Reuters reporting that Honeywell withdrew 2020 guidance on weak aviation demand supports that early-April interpretation.

primary_cause: Persistent fallout from suspended FY2020 guidance and COVID operational disruption. FedEx suspended its outlook on March 17 due to significant impact of coronavirus
secondary_factors: Unfavorable package mix service strain and recession fears
store_description: FedEx's 6.4% fall reflects investors still digesting its suspended 2020 outlook and the realization that pandemic package growth was not translating neatly into earnings because the network was under operational stress and commercial volumes were weakening.

primary_cause: Broad industrial/cyclical selloff. No material Emerson-specific headline in April 1-3
secondary_factors: Exposure to capital spending manufacturing slowdown and energy end markets
store_description: Emerson's 4.2% drop looks mainly like a cyclical-industrial reaction to the payroll shock and deepening recession fears. No fresh company-specific event so the most defensible explanation is macro plus its sensitivity to industrial capex and energy.

primary_cause: Broad market selloff. No material Duke-specific headline in April 1-3
secondary_factors: Utility demand concerns especially reduced commercial and industrial electricity usage during shutdowns
store_description: Duke's 4.2% decline appears macro-driven rather than headline-driven. Investors selling across the market after the payroll report with regulated utilities also vulnerable to worries about lower business demand and collections.

primary_cause: Fresh furlough announcement confirming the severity and duration of park/media shutdown pain. Disney said on April 2 it would furlough some U.S. employees beginning April 19
secondary_factors: ESPN disruption park closures film delays and the overall payroll-shock market selloff
store_description: Disney's 3.2% drop is best explained by its April 2 furlough announcement which told investors that shutdown pain was lasting longer than hoped. The need to furlough staff underscored how hard parks and related operations were being hit by COVID.

primary_cause: Anticipated surge in consumer credit losses from unemployment. Credit-sensitive lenders were under pressure as the labor-market collapse implied sharply higher card and consumer-loan losses
secondary_factors: Broad bank selloff card-loan exposure and recession fears
store_description: Capital One's 3.8% drop was very likely a forward-looking credit call. That logic was later validated when Capital One posted a $1.3 billion quarterly loss after building roughly $5.0 billion of reserves for anticipated credit problems.

primary_cause: Expected credit-loss reserve build from recession and rising unemployment. Large banks with credit-card exposure were being repriced for higher defaults. Citi later disclosed a $4.89 billion reserve build primarily in credit cards
secondary_factors: Global bank exposure broad financial-sector weakness and lower rates
store_description: Citigroup's 4.4% decline fits a straightforward early-pandemic bank trade. When Citi reported less than two weeks later it confirmed the market's fear by taking a $4.89 billion charge to bolster reserves against anticipated losses especially in cards.

primary_cause: Travel-and-entertainment spending collapse plus credit risk. American Express was directly exposed to collapsing travel and entertainment spend. Reuters later reported AmEx cut planned 2020 spending by nearly $3 billion
secondary_factors: General financials selloff and uncertainty around business travel recovery
store_description: AmEx fell 4.0% because investors were looking through to a business model unusually tied to travel corporate spend and affluent card activity all of which were suddenly impaired. Later disclosures showing a 3% drop in U.S. spending and 11% drop overseas support that interpretation.

primary_cause: Broad market and software multiple compression. No material Adobe-specific headline in April 1-3
secondary_factors: Concern about enterprise and SMB spending cuts during lockdowns despite Adobe's relatively strong recurring model
store_description: Adobe's 3.4% decline looks macro-driven rather than triggered by a fresh company event. High-quality software names were still selling off when recession fears spiked as investors worried even recurring-revenue businesses could see weaker new bookings.
